Glossary

pdmS7 documentation

Source: vignettes/glossary.Rmd
glossary.Rmd

Plain definitions of the terms used across this site. Each points to the article that explains it in full.

The model

PDM (Probability Distributed Model). A rainfall-runoff model that treats the catchment as a collection of soil stores of different sizes, so that part of it is saturated and runs off quickly while the rest absorbs rain (Moore, 2007). How the PDM works.

Store, or reservoir. A bucket of water in the model: the soil store, the surface stores and the groundwater store. Water drains from each at a rate set by how full it is.

Capacity distribution. How the sizes of the soil stores are spread across the catchment. The Pareto distribution is the usual choice; cmax is the largest store and b its shape. Choosing model components.

Saturated fraction. The share of the catchment whose stores are full, so that rain falling there runs straight off.

Recharge. Drainage from the soil store to groundwater, controlled by kg.

Routing. How stores turn the water they receive into a flow. The surface cascade (k1, k2) gives the quick response; the groundwater store (kb) the slow baseflow.

Time constant. The time a linear store takes to drain to about 37 per cent of its contents, in hours. Larger means slower.

Rainfall factor (fc). A multiplier on the rainfall the model receives. Values far from 1 usually point at the rain data rather than the catchment.

PACK. The snow model that can sit in front of the PDM, turning precipitation and temperature into rain and melt. How the snow model works.

State. The contents of every store at a moment. Warm-up is the period at the start of a run, simulated but not scored, while the stores settle from their starting state. Starting a run.

Response time. How quickly the model’s flow responds to rain: the time to peak after a pulse of rain, and the recession time as it drains. pdm_response_time(). Testing forecasts with hindcasts.

Water balance. Rain in equals evaporation, flow out and change in storage. pdmS7 checks it at every step.

Calibration

Calibration. Adjusting a model’s parameters so its flow matches measured flow. Automatic calibration, explained.

Bounds. The lowest and highest value each parameter may take during a calibration.

Objective. The score a calibration tries to make as small as possible, such as 1 - NSE.

Search scale. Whether a parameter is searched evenly in its own units or in its logarithm. Log scale suits parameters spanning orders of magnitude, such as kb.

Multi-start. Running the search from several starting points and keeping the best, so a single unlucky start does not decide the result.

Staged calibration. Calibrating groups of parameters in turn: the water balance and slow stores first, then the fast stores, then a joint polish. calibrate_staged().

Calibration, validation and test windows. Three separate periods. The model is fitted on the first, checked on the second, and scored once on the third after every choice is made. A split-sample test in Klemeš’s (1986) terms.

Wettest years held back. The two water years (October to September) with the highest flows, left out of calibration and validation and scored once with the test: a differential split-sample test, which checks the model on floods larger than those it was fitted to. Larger floods.

Highest gauged flow. The largest flow ever measured directly at a station. Above it the rating curve is extrapolated, so recorded flows there are uncertain in size.

Synthetic river. A calibration problem with a known answer: generated rain, a model with chosen parameters, and a simulated gauge. Synthetic rivers.

Rainfall generator. A random process that produces rain with realistic statistics: rectangular-pulse models (Neyman-Scott, Bartlett-Lewis), a Markov chain with gamma amounts, or resampling of a real record.

Structure. The choice of components: capacity distribution, recharge rule and routing. Choosing a model structure.

Equifinality. Different parameter sets giving almost equally good fits. It means the data do not pin those parameters down. A calibration project keeps up to 50 such equally good sets and runs them through the held-back years.

Batch calibration. Applying one calibration protocol to many catchments. Calibrating many catchments.

Scores

NSE (Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency). 1 minus the squared errors divided by the variance of the observed flow. 1 is perfect; 0 is no better than the mean flow. Dominated by floods. Scoring a simulation.

KGE (Kling-Gupta efficiency). Combines three terms: correlation (kge_r), the ratio of variability (kge_alpha) and the ratio of means (kge_beta). 1 is perfect.

Log NSE, log RMSE. The same scores on the logarithm of flow, which gives low flows weight.

Volume error. Total simulated flow over total observed, minus 1.

Flow-duration curve signatures. Biases in the high-flow, mid-range and low-flow parts of the flow-duration curve (fdc_high, fdc_mid, fdc_low).

Threshold. A flow or level that matters, such as a Flood Warning level.

POD (probability of detection). The share of observed threshold crossings the model also made. 1 is perfect.

FAR (false alarm ratio). The share of the model’s threshold crossings that did not happen. 0 is perfect.

CSI (critical success index). Hits divided by hits, misses and false alarms together: one number combining POD and FAR. 1 is perfect.

Event and step scores. Event scores count each episode above a threshold once; step scores count every time step.

Lower benchmark. A deliberately simple prediction, such as the mean flow for each day of the year, that any useful model must beat (Seibert et al., 2018).

Forecasting

Forecast origin. The moment a forecast is issued. Lead time is how far ahead of the origin a forecast value lies.

Updating. Using the latest observations at the origin to improve a forecast. Forecast updating.

State correction. Updating by adjusting the model’s stores at the origin.

Error, in forecasting. Observed minus simulated flow. A positive error means the model is too low.

AR and ARMA models. Autoregressive (and moving-average) models that predict how the recent error will carry on; the forecast is the simulation plus the predicted error. Post-processing is this correction applied after the model runs, as in IMFS. AR and ARMA error correction, explained.

Root, decay time. An AR model behaves like several fading processes added together, one per root; each root’s decay time is how long its part of the error takes to fade to 37 per cent.

Deltares convention. The sign convention for AR coefficients used by IMFS, reach.postproc and pdmS7. Moore (2007) writes the same coefficients with the opposite sign.

Hindcast. Rerunning past forecasts as if they were live, from many origins, using the rain that fell. Testing forecasts with hindcasts.

Persistence. The forecast that the river stays at its last measured flow. Skill is measured against it: 0 is no better than persistence, 1 is perfect.

Records and review

Calibration log. The append-only, checksummed record of a calibration. Logging a manual calibration.

Entry. One record in the log: project start, data registration, structure, trial, automatic calibration, note, candidate, validation, test, sign-off or reopen.

Checksum (MD5). A short fingerprint of a file. Any change to the file changes it, so a stored checksum proves the file is unchanged.

Candidate. The run the Custodian proposes as the final calibration.

Sign-off. A Steward’s recorded acceptance. Reviewing a calibration.

Owner, Steward, Custodian. The governance roles: accountable, reviewing and doing.

Run log and fingerprint. An optional record of every model run, each identified by a fingerprint of its configuration, so an operational run can be traced to the calibration that approved it.

Bronze, Silver, Gold. The tiers of the hydrometric data store in reach.io: raw as received, quality controlled, and approved products. Preparing your data.

Benchmarking

LSTM (long short-term memory network). A type of neural network used for rainfall-runoff modelling, usually trained on many catchments at once.

Benchmark protocol. The comparison of PDM and LSTM fixed in advance: data, periods, effort and scores. The protocol.

Simulation mode. Running a model without any observed flow at run time. Forecast mode uses observations at the origin.

CAMELS-GB. An open dataset of 671 catchments in Great Britain with daily data and catchment attributes (Coxon et al., 2020).

Stratum. A group of catchments, such as the third with the highest baseflow index, over which results are summarised.
